imageDescription: Schiele, with wild hair and a tilted head, looks sideways out of the picture beside a plant with red lantern-shaped fruit.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Egon Schiele painted this self-portrait in 1912, aged 22. He turns his head sharply, staring sideways out of the picture, his face drawn with angular lines and strange colours. Beside him grows a physalis, or Chinese lantern plant, with red husks. It was painted as a pair with a portrait of his partner, Wally Neuzil, and the two hang side by side. Schiele's raw, expressive style shocked Vienna and influenced Expressionism. He died of flu in 1918, at 28, three days after his wife. It belongs to the Leopold Museum in Vienna.

imageDescription: Large yellow and orange petal shapes, spirals, circles and letters float on a lilac ground.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Hilma af Klint painted The Ten Largest series in 1907, years before the famous pioneers of abstract art. These huge paintings, over three metres tall, trace the stages of human life from childhood to old age; No. 7 represents adulthood. Petal shapes, spirals, circles and letters float on a lilac ground. Af Klint, a trained Swedish painter, believed spirit guides she contacted in séances directed the work. She asked that these paintings not be shown until at least 20 years after her death. Exhibitions since the 1980s have transformed the story of abstract art. They belong to the Hilma af Klint Foundation.

title: Woman with a Hat
collection: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art

statements.text: Fauvism, after a critic called the painters "wild beasts."

imageDescription: A woman in a huge, wildly coloured hat, her face painted in streaks of green, blue and orange.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Henri Matisse painted this portrait of his wife, Amélie, in 1905. Her face is streaked with green, blue and orange, and her enormous hat is a riot of loose, bright patches of colour. Matisse used colour for its emotional force rather than to describe what he saw. When it was shown at the Salon d'Automne in Paris that year, a critic called Matisse and his friends "les fauves," the wild beasts, and Fauvism was born. Gertrude and Leo Stein bought it, launching their famous collection. It belongs to the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art.

imageDescription: A woman arranges fruit on a table in a room where the red tablecloth and red wall share the same blue pattern; a window shows a garden.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Henri Matisse painted The Dessert: Harmony in Red in 1908 for the Moscow collector Sergei Shchukin. A woman arranges fruit on a table in a room where the red wall and red tablecloth share the same blue pattern of plants and baskets, so the space flattens into decoration. Through the window, a garden of trees in blossom offers a cool green contrast. Matisse first painted it in blue, as Harmony in Blue, then repainted it red. After the Russian Revolution, Shchukin's collection was taken by the state. It belongs to the Hermitage in St Petersburg.

title: Street, Dresden
collection: Museum of Modern Art, New York

rounds.hint: What did the Nazis call his work?

imageDescription: Crowds with masklike faces push along a pink street, a woman in a huge hat in front and a tram behind.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner painted Street, Dresden in 1908. Crowds with masklike faces push along a lurid pink street, a woman in a huge hat at the front and a tram behind. The colours and distortions express the anxiety and alienation of modern city life rather than its appearance. Kirchner co-founded Die Brücke, The Bridge, a group of German Expressionists who wanted art to be raw and direct. The Nazis later called his work "degenerate" and removed it from museums, and Kirchner took his own life in 1938. It belongs to the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

title: The Large Blue Horses

statements.why: Klee joined later; Kandinsky co-founded it.

imageDescription: Three blue horses with curving bodies stand together before red and yellow hills.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Franz Marc painted The Large Blue Horses in 1911. Three blue horses with sweeping, curved bodies stand together before red and yellow hills. Marc gave colours meanings: blue stood for the spiritual and the masculine. He loved animals as images of purity and harmony with nature. That year he co-founded Der Blaue Reiter, The Blue Rider, in Munich with Wassily Kandinsky, a group devoted to the spiritual in art. Marc was killed at Verdun in 1916, aged 36, and the Nazis later called his work degenerate. It belongs to the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis.

collection: Museum of Modern Art, New York

imageDescription: A giant red horse and straining workers blur together in a whirl of energy at a city building site.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Umberto Boccioni painted The City Rises in 1910. A giant red horse and straining workers blur into a whirl of energy on a building site on the edge of Milan, where new factories and a power station are rising. Boccioni was a leading figure of Futurism, an Italian movement that celebrated speed, machines, the modern city and even violence, and rejected the art of the past. He wanted the painting to show movement and noise rather than a still moment. He died in 1916 after falling from a horse during army training. It belongs to MoMA.

title: Portrait of Pablo Picasso

statements.text: Pablo Picasso, Gris's friend and neighbour.
statements.why: They lived in the same Paris building.

statements.text: Gris from Portugal, Picasso from Spain.

imageDescription: Picasso's head and body broken into faceted blue, grey and brown planes, holding a palette.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Juan Gris painted this portrait of Pablo Picasso in 1912. Picasso's head and body are broken into faceted planes of blue, grey and brown, and he holds a palette. Gris was a fellow Spaniard and neighbour in the same Paris studio building, and he wrote a dedication on the canvas: "Homage to Pablo Picasso." The portrait shows Cubism, the movement Picasso and Braque invented, at its most clear and orderly. It was the painting Gris chose for his first public exhibition. Gris died in 1927, aged only 40. It belongs to the Art Institute of Chicago.

statements.text: The Flood and the Last Judgement.

imageDescription: An explosion of colours, lines and shapes swirls across a large canvas with no recognisable objects.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Wassily Kandinsky painted Composition VII in 1913, after making more than 30 drawings, watercolours and oil studies. The final canvas, about two by three metres, was then painted in just a few days. An explosion of colours, lines and shapes swirls across it, with no recognisable objects, though themes such as the Flood, the Resurrection and the Last Judgement lie behind it. Kandinsky compared colours to musical notes and gave his most important works musical titles, painting ten Compositions in all. It is often called his masterpiece. It belongs to the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow.

imageDescription: Overlapping coloured circles of many sizes float on a dark background, the largest black with a blue halo.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Wassily Kandinsky painted Several Circles in 1926, while teaching at the Bauhaus in Germany. Overlapping coloured circles of many sizes float on a dark background, mixing where they cross like transparent films, while a large black circle glows with a blue halo. Kandinsky called the circle the most modest yet the most assertive of forms, and saw it as a link to the cosmos. The painting looks like a view of planets and stars, though it is purely abstract. Solomon R. Guggenheim collected Kandinsky widely, and the painting belongs to the Guggenheim Museum in New York.

title: Black Square

statements.text: High in a corner, where Russian homes hung icons.

imageDescription: A black square, its surface covered in fine cracks, on a white ground.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Kazimir Malevich painted Black Square in 1915 and showed it at an exhibition in Petrograd, hung high in a corner where Russian homes traditionally placed a religious icon. A black square on a white ground, it was meant as a zero point for painting, freed from depicting the world. Malevich called his movement Suprematism. Over time the black paint has cracked, and researchers have found an earlier painting underneath. He painted four Black Squares in all. Under Stalin, such abstract art was suppressed. This first version belongs to the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow.

imageDescription: The branches of a tree spread across the canvas in grey and black curves, almost dissolving into a pattern.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Piet Mondrian painted Gray Tree in 1911. The branches of a tree spread across the canvas in rhythmic grey and black curves, almost dissolving into a pattern of lines and planes. It belongs to a series of tree paintings in which Mondrian moved step by step from realistic landscape toward pure abstraction, influenced by Cubism, which he saw in Paris. Within a few years, the curves would become the straight black lines and primary colours of his famous later work. When he moved to Paris he dropped an "a" from his name. It belongs to the Kunstmuseum Den Haag.

imageDescription: A large red square dominates a white grid divided by thick black lines, with a blue block at bottom left and a small yellow one at bottom right.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Piet Mondrian painted Composition II in Red, Blue and Yellow in 1930. A large red square dominates a white grid divided by thick black lines, balanced by a blue block at the bottom left and a small yellow one at the bottom right. Mondrian limited himself to primary colours, black, white and grey, and to horizontal and vertical lines, seeking a universal harmony. He split from a fellow De Stijl artist who introduced diagonals. His style later influenced fashion, design and architecture. He moved to New York in 1940 and died there in 1944. It belongs to the Kunsthaus Zürich.

imageDescription: A crowded collage of flat, bright shapes, stencilled letters, scaffolding, a purple pole and robot-like figures on stairs.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Fernand Léger painted The City in 1919, soon after serving in the First World War, where he was gassed at Verdun. The war gave him a fascination with machines and modern technology. The large canvas is a crowded collage of flat, bright shapes: scaffolding, stencilled letters like those on posters, a purple pole and robotic figures climbing stairs. It captures the noise, speed and visual chaos of the modern city, like a billboard. Léger later worked on murals, film and stage design. It belongs to the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

title: Twittering Machine
medium: Watercolour and oil transfer on paper
collection: Museum of Modern Art, New York

statements.text: With an oil-transfer drawing technique and watercolour.

statements.why: It was sold off from a German museum.

imageDescription: Thin black lines draw four strange birds perched on a wire attached to a hand crank, over a misty blue-pink background.
credit: Image: public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
summary: Paul Klee made Twittering Machine in 1922, using an oil-transfer drawing technique, like carbon paper, combined with watercolour. Thin black lines draw four strange birds perched on a wire attached to a hand crank, over a misty blue-to-pink background. It is playful and unsettling at once, a mechanical toy that perhaps traps the birds into singing. Klee taught at the Bauhaus. In 1937 the Nazis seized the work from a German museum as "degenerate," and the Museum of Modern Art in New York bought it in 1939. Today it is one of his best-known images.

title: Jeanne Hébuterne
collection: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

statements.text: Modigliani's partner and the mother of his daughter.
A long oval face and almond eyes.

rounds.hint: Where did his long necks come from?

imageDescription: A young woman with a long neck and an oval face rests her head on her hand, leaning on a chair.
credit: Image: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, public domain (CC0)
summary: Amedeo Modigliani painted Jeanne Hébuterne, his partner and the mother of his daughter, many times; this portrait dates from 1919. She rests her head on her hand, with Modigliani's signature long neck, oval face and almond-shaped eyes, influenced by African and ancient Cycladic sculpture. The couple lived in poverty in Paris. Modigliani died of tuberculosis in January 1920, aged 35, and two days later Jeanne, heavily pregnant, took her own life. She was 21. His work became valuable only after his death. It belongs to the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
